title: 12. Model Context Protocol - MCP
text:
MCP - Model Context Protocol

MCP (Model Context Protocol) is an open-source standard for connecting AI applications to external systems. (https://modelcontextprotocol.io/docs/getting-started/intro)
Proposed by Anthropic in November 2024

Using MCP, AI applications like Claude or ChatGPT can connect to data sources (e.g. local files, databases), tools (e.g. search engines, calculators) and workflows (e.g. specialized prompts)—enabling them to access key information and perform tasks.

title: 12. Model Context Protocol - MCP
text:
What can MCP enable? (examples)

Agents can access your Google Calendar and Notion, acting as a more personalized AI assistant.
Claude Code can generate an entire web app using a Figma design.
Enterprise chatbots can connect to multiple databases across an organization, empowering users to analyze data using chat.
AI models can create 3D designs on Blender and print them out using a 3D printer.

title: 12. Model Context Protocol - MCP
text:
Why does MCP matter?

Developers: MCP reduces development time and complexity when building, or integrating with, an AI application or agent.
AI applications or agents: MCP provides access to an ecosystem of data sources, tools and apps which will enhance capabilities and improve the end-user experience.
End-users: MCP results in more capable AI applications or agents which can access your data and take actions on your behalf when necessary.

title: 12. Model Context Protocol - MCP
text:
MCP example - Context7

“Context7” is the name of a specific software platform and Model Context Protocol (MCP) server designed to provide up-to-date, version-specific documentation and code examples to AI coding assistants and Large Language Models (LLMs)
Key aspects of Context7 include:

Accurate Information: It extracts high-quality, relevant code snippets from official documentation sources (like Markdown, plain text, or Jupyter notebooks), ensuring the AI works with the latest APIs and best practices.
Integration: It works with various AI clients and IDEs that support the Model Context Protocol (MCP).
Ease of Use: Developers can often trigger it within their prompts by simply adding the phrase “use context7” to a query in a compatible editor.
Problem Solver: It addresses the challenge of AI models having knowledge cutoffs, which makes them unaware of recent library updates, new features, or breaking changes.

title: 12. Model Context Protocol - MCP
text:
MCP and AI Agents

MCPs are the agent’s tools

title: 12. Model Context Protocol - MCP
text:
MCP vs. API

APIs are the old way (or used to be) — powerful, but not built for AI.
MCP is the new standard — dynamic, self-describing, and AI-native.
API – software to software
MCP – for LLMs to fetch context and tools
While APIs are an interface meant to utilized by developers, MCP is an interface/wrapper around APIs meant to be utilized by LLMs.
Or at least API was the old (last year) - we are starting to use APIs again over MCP - why?

title: 12. Model Context Protocol - MCP
text:
MCP vs. API



Discovery – ask the MCP for its tools
Unlike traditional APIs, where every integration is custom, MCP standardizes the interface.
An AI agent can interact with any MCP-compatible service without needing prior knowledge of its specifics.
API creates breaking changes. MCP can be used immediately.

title: 12. Model Context Protocol - MCP
text:
Two Core Problems MCP Solves

LLMs need two things from external systems:

Context — Structured data (documents, database records, knowledge bases).
Tools — Actions they can perform (search the web, send an email, run code).

title: 12. Model Context Protocol - MCP
text:
Dynamic discovery

AI agents can ask a server what it can do at runtime

An MCP client sends a request like tools/list to discover available functions.
The server responds with descriptions, input/output formats, and usage examples.
The AI can then invoke those tools without pre-programmed integration.

title: 12. Model Context Protocol - MCP
text:
CLI vs. MCP — The Trade-off

MCP is great for discovery and standardization
But MCP servers are token-heavy — schema definitions eat context fast
Example:

A single GitHub MCP integration uses ~55,000 tokens just for tool definitions
CLI tools use ~4,150 tokens for the same task — a 35x reduction

More tokens used on tools = less room for actual reasoning

title: 8. Graph RAG
text:
Issues with Naive RAGs





Loss of Context: Splitting documents into independent chunks severs the relationships between them
Difficulty with Comparative Questions: Answering “What are the differences between Product A and Product B?” is hard
Redundancy and Noise: Multiple chunks saying roughly the same thing add noise for the LLM
“Shallow” Retrieval: Vector search finds explicit information but struggles with implicit relationships. It will not know that “MIT” is a “university” in “Cambridge” unless that is stated in the chunk

Zettelkasten

En note-metode fra 1900-tallet — opfundet af sociolog Niklas Luhmann
Han producerede 90.000 håndskrevne noter og over 70 bøger
Princip: Én idé per note, altid linket til relaterede noter
Noter er ikke hierarkiske mapper — de er et netværk af tanker
De tre note-typer:

Fleeting notes — hurtige tanker, kasseres efter bearbejdning
Literature notes — hvad du lærte fra en kilde, med egne ord
Permanent notes — din egen indsigt, formuleret til at stå alene

Graph RAGs

Based on graphs instead of vectors
Instead of a list of text chunks, we first build a Knowledge Graph
The graph explicitly stores entities as nodes and relationships between them as edges

title: 8. Graph RAG
text:
Building the Graph

This isn’t just about embedding text — it’s about extracting structured information from unstructured text
We identify the key entities and how they connect
Example: From the sentence “Dr. Eva Core developed the ‘Helios’ project at InnoTech”:

Three nodes: Eva Core, Helios, InnoTech
Two relationships: DEVELOPED, WORKED_AT

title: 8. Graph RAG
text:
Combining Vector + Graph RAG

Vector search: fast semantic similarity — great for finding relevant content
Graph traversal: structured relationship queries — great for finding connected context
Hybrid: use vector search to find the entry point, then traverse the graph to enrich the answer

title: 8. Graph RAG
text: ETL for Graph RAGs

title: 8. Graph RAG
text:
Extract

Entity Extraction: Use LLMs to identify key entities in your documents

People, organisations, locations, topics, etc.

Relationship Extraction: Identify verbs or phrases that connect entities

“Company X acquired Company Y”
“Person A is the CEO of Company B”

title: 8. Graph RAG
text:
Transform

Schema Definition: Define what types of nodes and relationships your graph will have

Node types: Person, Company, Project
Relationship types: WORKS_FOR, ACQUIRED, TOPIC_OF

Data Cleaning & Normalisation: Standardise entity names

“MIT” and “Massachusetts Institute of Technology” → same node

title: 8. Graph RAG
text:
Load

Populate the Graph Database: Use a graph database like Neo4j to load the extracted nodes and relationships
Creates the persistent, queryable knowledge graph the RAG system will use

title: 8. Graph RAG
text:
Using the Graph DB

Query Transformation: Natural language question → formal graph query (Cypher), done with an LLM

MATCH (p:Project {name: 'Helios'})-[:HAS_FEATURE]->(f:Feature)
RETURN f.name

Graph Traversal & Retrieval: The DB returns a structured subgraph — not just a chunk of text, but related nodes and edges
Context Augmentation: The structured data is serialised into readable text and passed to the LLM as context

title: 8. Graph RAG
text:
Example: Course Prerequisites
Naïve RAG query: “Which courses should I take after Databases?”

A vector RAG might return the description of an advanced database course — and that’s it

Graph RAG query: Same question → transformed to Cypher:
MATCH (:Course {name: 'Databases'})-[:IS_PREREQUISITE_FOR]->(c:Course)
RETURN c.name

Returns all courses with Databases as a prerequisite
Can also pull in descriptions — a complete, accurate answer

title: 8. Graph RAG
text:
Use Case: Code Base Navigation
Nodes: Functions, Classes, Files, Modules, Developers
Relationships: CALLS, DEFINED_IN, IMPORTS, AUTHORED_BY
Questions a Graph RAG can answer:

“What does the calculate_metrics function do?” → retrieves docstring + code
“Who has modified user_authentication.py the most?” → traverse AUTHORED_BY and aggregate
“Show all functions that call database.connect()” → trivial graph query, very hard for vector search

Single-Agent Systems (SAS)



Definition

Single-Agent System (SAS): A system where one AI agent performs tasks sequentially without collaboration.

Characteristics

Sequential Execution: Tasks are completed one after another.
Single Context Window: Limited by the agent’s context size (risk of “context rot”).
No Parallelism: All computation happens in one agent.

Limitations of Single-Agent Systems (SAS)

Limitation: If the agent’s ‘memory’ (context) gets full, it might forget early details!

Finite sizeof context window (even with 1M+ tokens).
“Context rot”: Performance drops as context fills up.

“Problem”: Brain Overload
Imagine trying to remember 10 books at once—you’d mix up details!
A single agent faces the same issue with too much data.


Sequential Tasks:

SAS excels when tasks depend on prior steps (e.g., analysis → design → coding).

Definition: Multiple AI agents collaborating to solve tasks.

Each agent focuses on one task, like a team of specialists

Parallel processing (e.g., research agents).
Specialization (e.g., agents with curated tools).
Mitigates “context rot” (performance drop in large context windows).

Agents need to share data to collaborate effectively.

Shared Memory

Agent Communication II

Direct Messages


Agents send updates or requests to each other.

Example: Agent 1: “Here’s the data!” → Agent 2: “Thanks! Here’s the analysis.”

Task Lists


Agents pick tasks from a shared list.

Example: A Trello board where agents claim tasks like “Research X” or “Code Y.”
Pros: Avoids duplication.
Cons: Requires a manager for the list.

What Are Skills?

Why Skills Matter

Modularity: Agents can mix/match skills for different tasks.
Reusability: Skills can be shared across agents (e.g., a “web search” skill for all agents).
Specialization: Agents can have unique skill sets (e.g., a “coder agent” with GitHub tools).

How Agents Use Skills

Skill Execution Flow

Trigger: Agent decides a skill is needed (e.g., “I need data for this report”).
Tool Use: Agent calls the skill (e.g., runs a web search).
Result Integration: Agent uses the output (e.g., summarizes search results).

Skills:

title: 6. multi agents and vibe coding
text:
Designing Effective Skills

Best Practices

Single Purpose: One skill = one task (e.g., “search web” vs. “search and summarize”).
Clear Inputs/Outputs:


Input: “Query for web search.”
Output: “List of URLs and snippets.”


Error Handling: Skills should fail gracefully (e.g., retry or alert the agent).

Pitfalls to Avoid

Overlapping Skills: Two skills doing the same thing (e.g., “search web” and “Google search”).
Complex Skills: Skills that do too much (e.g., “write a full report”) → harder to debug.
No Feedback: Skills should return useful errors (e.g., “No results found” vs. crashing).

Vibe coding
Vibe coding is a relative new paradigm where the programmer’s “vibe” or intention drives the AI’s code generation, relying on prompt iteration and output testing rather than traditional code authoring and review

title: 6. multi agents and vibe coding
text:
What is vibe coding?

Natural Language Input: Programmers describe their requirements in everyday language, like “build a user login page.” AI then translates this into functional code, often without the developer looking at or editing the generated code directly.​
AI as Coding Partner: The human role focuses on guiding, testing, and providing feedback, rather than worrying about implementation details and syntax. The process is often iterative—adjustments are made by refining the instructions rather than the code.​
Acceptance Without Full Understanding: True “vibe coding” means embracing the AI’s suggestions without thorough manual review or understanding of the codebase, in contrast to traditional pair programming or code-completion tools where the developer remains tightly involved with the output.​

title: 6. multi agents and vibe coding
text:
Why vibe coding?

Faster Prototyping: Vibe coding accelerates app building, making it possible for those with less coding experience to develop complex software rapidly.​
Risks and Criticisms: While this method opens software development to more people and speeds up prototyping, there are concerns about maintainability, accountability, and security—especially since developers might deploy code they do not fully understand.

Typical Vibe Coding Workflow

State what’s needed in plain English​
Let the AI generate, test, and refine the code​
Repeat and iterate by updating prompts or goals​
Focus on output and function, not on syntax or structure

Self-Attention

Self-attention allows a model to weigh the importance of different words in a sentence when processing a particular word

For example: “The robot picked up the red ball because it was the right color,”self-attention helps the model understand that “it” refers to the “ball” and not the “robot.” 

For each word, the model can “look” at all other words in the input sequence and determine which ones are most relevant to understanding its meaning in that specific context
This ability to capture relationships between words, regardless of their distance from each other in the sentence, is a key advantage over sequential models

LLM  limitations

Hallucinations : LLMs can generate plausible but incorrect or nonsensical information.
Bias : They can reflect and amplify biases present in their training data.
Lack of True Understanding : At their core, LLMs are probabilistic models predicting the next token; they do not possess true consciousness or understanding in the human sense.
Computational Cost : Training and deploying large-scale LLMs requires significant computational resources.

title: 4. Large Language Models
text:
Temperature

Temperature is a key parameter that controls the randomness of an LLM’s output.
It’s a value, typically between 0 and 2, that you can set when you make a request to the model.
Think of it as a dial for creativity.
Low Temperature (e.g., 0.1 to 0.5): With a low temperature, the model becomes more deterministic and conservative.
High Temperature (e.g., 0.8 to 1.5): A higher temperature increases the chances of the model selecting less likely tokens.

title: 4. Large Language Models
text:
More temperature

Not True Creativity : While a higher temperature can lead to more novel-sounding outputs, it’s not the same as human creativity. It’s simply increasing the mathematical randomness of the word selection.[10][15] The model’s inherent creativity is more tied to its architecture and training data.[15]
Risk of Incoherence : Pushing the temperature too high can result in nonsensical or “hallucinated” outputs that don’t make sense.[7]
Finding the Balance : The right temperature setting depends entirely on the task at hand. For a reliable AI agent performing a predictable task, a low temperature is generally preferred.[10] For an agent designed to brainstorm or explore possibilities, a higher temperature might be more appropriate.[9]

title: 4. Large Language Models
text:
Top-K Sampling

Definition: Filters the probability distribution to keep only the top k most likely tokens.
Process:

Sort all possible next words by their probability.
Keep only the top k options (e.g., if k=40, only the 40 most likely words are considered).
Redistribute the probability mass among these k tokens.
Randomly sample the next word from this restricted set.

Impact:

Pros: Very simple and prevents the model from picking completely nonsensical “long-tail” words.
Cons: It is not adaptive. If the model is very confident (one word is 99%), it still looks at the other 39. If the model is uncertain, it might cut off valid, high-quality choices.

title: 4. Large Language Models
text:
Top-P (Nucleus) Sampling


Definition: A dynamic approach that selects the smallest set of tokens whose cumulative probability exceeds a threshold p.
Process:

Sort all possible next words by probability.
Add words to a “nucleus” one by one until their combined probability reaches p (e.g., p=0.9 or 90%).
The number of words in the set grows or shrinks based on the model’s confidence.
Sample the next word only from this “nucleus.”

Impact:

Pros: Adaptive. When the model is confident, the set is small (maybe 1 word); when it’s confused, the set is large.
Cons: Harder to predict exactly how many options the model will have at any given step.

Often considered superior to Top-K for maintaining a natural and creative “flow” in conversation.

Deterministic
The Traditional Way

Rules-based: “If This, Then That.”
Fixed Paths: Every step is pre-defined.
Predictable: Given the same input, you always get the same output.
Analogy: A train on tracks.


Agentic
The AI-Powered Way

Dynamic Paths: The AI decides which tools to use in real-time.
Flexible: Can handle unexpected data or “fuzzy” logic.
Analogy: A taxi driver.

The n8n Interface


The n8n dashboard is designed to be intuitive and visual.

Workflow Canvas: The main area where you build. It is an infinite digital whiteboard for your logic.
Nodes Panel: Located on the right (opened via the “+” button). This is your library of 400+ integrations and core tools.
Sidebar: Your command center for navigating between your workflow list, credentials, and execution history.
Settings: Accessible via the gear icon in the sidebar for environment variables and owner settings.

title: 2. Introduction to n8n
text:
Core Pillars: Workflows & Nodes


To master n8n, you must understand these three core concepts:

Workflows: A sequence of nodes connected together. A workflow always starts with a Trigger (e.g., a schedule, a webhook, or a manual “chat” prompt).
Nodes: The building blocks. Each node performs one specific action (e.g., “Send an Email,” “Ask ChatGPT,” or “Update Google Sheet”).
Parameters: The configuration inside a node (e.g., which email address to send to).

title: 2. Introduction to n8n

JSON vs. Binary Data
I n8n arbejder vi primært med to datatyper:

JSON (Struktureret data):

Tekst, tal, lister og objekter.
Det du ser i tabeller og “Schema”-visning.
Bruges til logik, filtre og API-kald.

Binary (Filer):

Billeder, PDF’er, Excel-filer, lyd.
Kan ikke læses direkte som tekst af n8n’s standard-logik.
Kræver specifikke nodes (f.eks. “Extract from File”) for at blive transformeret til JSON.

title: Two-week project
text:
A vector database finds what’s similar. A graph database knows what’s connected. Most real problems need both. Your task: pick a domain you care about, feed it into both databases, and build an agent that uses them together. The result is a retrieval system that’s more than the sum of its parts.


Through this project you will gain hands-on experience with:

Setting up and populating a vector database and a graph database.
Understanding when to use semantic search vs. graph traversal — and combining both.
Building data ingestion pipelines in n8n.
Building an AI agent that uses multiple knowledge sources as tools.





Choose a domain/case — pick something where both structured relationships (graph) and semantic similarity (vector) are useful
Set up a vector database (Neo4j)
Set up a graph database (Neo4j)
Build a workflow that ingests data into both databases
Build an AI agent that uses both databases as tools to answer questions

Examples of good cases:








Domain
Graph (relationships)
Vector (semantic search)




YouTube channel
Videos → topics, series, tags, related videos
Find videos similar to this one by content


Games
Games → genre, franchise, developer, platform
Find games that feel like “Dark Souls but more relaxed”


Recipes
Recipes → ingredients, cuisine, technique, dietary tags
Find something “creamy and quick”


Movies
Movies → director, actors, franchise, sequels
Find films with a similar vibe to this one


Research papers
Papers → authors, citations, topics
Find papers on similar themes


Music
Songs → artist, album, genre, collaborations
Find songs with a similar feel


Course material
Topics → lectures, articles, videos, concepts
Find content that explains this concept differently



A good case has both: some explicit structure you want to traverse (graph) and rich text/descriptions where meaning matters more than keywords (vector).
Think about what role your agent should play — an expert you can query, a tutor that guides you, a recommendation engine, a research assistant. The role shapes your prompt and what “a good answer” looks like.






Set up a vector database for text and vectors. Use Neo4j.
Use Ollama (local) or an OpenAI embedding model
Find a way to “chunk” your content - number of chars per chunk or does it have a useful structure already (e.g. text sections)
Create a workflow that populate the vector db with your text i.e. embeds the text and add to Neo4j
Consider adding meta data/attributes such as document where it is from
Automate the embedding with a n8n workflow inc. reading documents
You might want to check for duplicates (and even wipe the db if you restart your embedding)





Use Neo4j for the graph DB - same DB as the vector DB
Use AI to suggest node and relationship types
You have to make sure the nodes and relationships make sense for your case (normalise them)
Have an AI make cypher so you can import data to the DB - make it part of your workflow if possible - or use a cli like Claude code, codex, Gemini CLI or Mistral Vibe to do it
Make an n8n workflow that automate the import of the data to the DB





Have an AI Agent in the workflow
Add the vector and graph DB as tools to the agent - if you use weaker LLMs for the agent you might have to get the data from the vector and graph database and feed it to the agent (serial setup instead of tools)
Make a prompt for the AI agent so it responds as a specific role (expert in your area, tutor, or whatever makes sense), instruct it to do what you need it to do, have guardrails, etc





Add additional/new text/documents automatically to the DBs
Human in the loop — give the AI feedback to improve answers
Multi-agents — introduce an extra AI Agent that can evaluate the RAG Agent’s answers/output and give it feedback, preferably based on RAG information
Add references (agent shows which nodes/documents it used)

Chat interface (n8n’s built-in)

Hybrid search — combine vector + graph results in a single query rather than separately

title: Final project
text:
In the final project you will design, build and evaluate an AI agent system for a case of your own choice.
The purpose of the project is to apply the concepts from the course in a realistic use case. You are not expected to build a complete agent framework from scratch. You are expected to design a bounded system that uses agents, tools, workflows and retrieval in a meaningful way.
You must choose a relevant case yourself and justify it. The project should result in a working system. It should not just be a sandbox or toy demo. You must test the system and show that it works in your chosen case.

title: Final project
text:
Project type
This is an individual project. You can help each other, but you have to turn in your own project.

title: Final project
text:
Scope
You must build a prototype of an AI agent system for a case of your own choice.
You must use NanoClaw or Hermes Agent. If you want to use a different platform, you must get approval from the teacher first.
The project is about building a useful and bounded AI agent system for a real use case.

text:

title: Final project
text:
Functional requirements
Your system must:

support a clearly defined use case
use Neo4j vector RAG to retrieve relevant information from your corpus or project data
use Neo4j graph RAG to represent and use relationships between concepts, sources, requirements, arguments or tasks
expose at least one n8n workflow or RAG through an MCP server, so the agent can call it as a tool
support interaction with the user through a reasonable interface (e.g. Telegram, Discord, email, ..) Where the case calls for it, the system may use multiple agents with defined roles (e.g. an orchestrator and sub-agents). This is not required.

The exact functions of the system depend on your chosen case. The important thing is that the agent system solves a relevant problem in a meaningful way and that MCP, n8n, vector RAG and graph RAG are used as real parts of the solution.
Examples of relevant cases are:

a thesis or academic project support agent that tracks requirements, retrieves sources and monitors progress
a software development support agent that tracks issues, retrieves documentation and coordinates code reviews
a research assistant that manages literature, identifies gaps and summarizes findings
a customer support agent that retrieves product knowledge, handles common queries and escalates through workflows
a project management agent that tracks tasks, deadlines and team actions across a defined project
a content production assistant that tracks sources, story outlines and editorial tasks
a game companion agent that retrieves lore and guides, tracks quests or objectives and maps relationships between characters, factions and items in a chosen game
a personal trainer agent that tracks workouts and progress, retrieves training plans and nutrition guidance and maps relationships between goals, exercises and recovery

title: AI-Agenter-F2026
text:
Issues with Naïve RAGs
Loss of Context : When you split documents into independent chunks, you sever the relationships between them.
Difficulty with Comparative Questions : Answering questions like “What are the differences between Product A and Product B?” is hard.
Redundancy and Noise : You often retrieve multiple chunks that say roughly the same thing, or chunks that are only tangentially related to your query. This adds noise for the LLM to sift through.
“Shallow” Retrieval : Vector search is great at finding explicit information but struggles with implicit relationships. It won’t know that “MIT” is a “university” located in “Cambridge” unless that’s explicitly stated in the retrieved chunk.
![A diagram of a graph
AI-generated content may be incorrect.](./slides/lec9_files/ppt/media/image4.png “Picture 3”)

title: AI-Agenter-F2026
text:
What is a graph?
A graph is a data structure that models entities and the relationships between them

It is not a chart or coordinate system!

Nodes -  the primary “things” or nouns in your data.
Examples:

Person: “Dr. Eva Core”
Company: “InnoTech”
Project: “Helios”
Concept: “Machine Learning”

Relations - t he connections that give context to the nodes.
They are directed and labeled to describe the relationship.
Examples:

WORKS_AT
DEVELOPED
IS_PREREQUISITE_FOR




Graphs in Computer Science

title: AI-Agenter-F2026
text:
Graph RAGs
Based on graphs instead of vectors
Instead of a simple list of text chunks, we first build a Knowledge Graph.
This graph explicitly stores entities (like people, products, concepts) as nodes and the relationships between them as edges.”



A crash course on RAG systems—Part 7 - by Avi Chawla

title: AI-Agenter-F2026
text:
Building the graph
This isn’t just about embedding text.
It’s about extracting structured information from unstructured text.
We identify the key entities and how they connect.
For example, from the sentence ‘Dr. Eva Core developed the ’Helios’ project at InnoTech,’ we extract three nodes (Eva Core, Helios, InnoTech) and two relationships (DEVELOPED, WORKED_AT).”
![A diagram of a group of people
AI-generated content may be incorrect.](./slides/lec9_files/ppt/media/image7.jpeg “Picture 3”)

title: AI-Agenter-F2026
text:
ETL for Graph RAGs
Extract :
Entity Extraction: Use models (e.g. LLMs) to identify key entities (people, organizations, locations, topics, etc.) in your documents.
Relationship Extraction: This is the crucial part. Identify the verbs or phrases that connect these entities. For example, “Company X acquired Company Y,” “Person A is the CEO of Company B.”
Transform :
Schema Definition: Define your graph schema. What types of nodes will you have (e.g., Person, Company, Project)? What types of relationships (WORKS_FOR, ACQUIRED, TOPIC_OF)?
Data Cleaning & Normalization: Standardize entity names (“MIT” and “Massachusetts Institute of Technology” should be the same node).
Load :
Populate the Graph Database: Use a graph database like Neo4j to load the extracted nodes and relationships. This creates the persistent, queryable knowledge graph that the RAG system will use..



Understand What is ETL: Extract, Transform, Load Explained

title: AI-Agenter-F2026
text:
Using the graph DB
Query Transformation: The user’s natural language question (“What are the main features of Project Helios?”) is transformed into a formal graph query (e.g., Cypher for Neo4j). This can be done using an LLM.

Example Cypher Query: MATCH ( p:Project {name: ‘Helios’})-[:HAS_FEATURE]->( f:Feature ) RETURN f.name

Graph Traversal & Retrieval:

The graph DB executes this query, retrieving not just a single piece of text, but a structured subgraph of related information.
You might retrieve the project node, its features, the team members who worked on it, and links to related documentation.

Context Augmentation:

This structured information is then serialized into a clean, readable format and passed to the LLM as context, along with the original question. The LLM gets a pre-digested summary of all the relevant, interconnected facts.

title: AI-Agenter-F2026
text:
Example of use
The RAG in Action:

Naïve RAG Query : “Which courses should I take after Databases?” A vector RAG might return the description of the advanced database course, but that’s it.
Graph RAG Query : Ask the same question. Show how the Graph RAG transforms this into a Cypher query: MATCH (:Course {name: ‘Databases’})-[:IS_PREREQUISITE_FOR]->( c:Course ) RETURN c.name.
The Result : The Graph RAG will definitively list all courses that have Databases as a prerequisite. It can also pull in their descriptions, providing a complete and accurate answer that the vector search might miss.

Vibe coding
Vibe coding is a new paradigm where the programmer’s “vibe” or intention drives the AI’s code generation, relying on prompt iteration and output testing rather than traditional code authoring and review

title: AI-Agenter-F2026
text:
What is vibe coding?
Natural Language Input : Programmers describe their requirements in everyday language, like “build a user login page.” AI then translates this into functional code, often without the developer looking at or editing the generated code directly.
AI as Coding Partner : The human role focuses on guiding, testing, and providing feedback, rather than worrying about implementation details and syntax. The process is often iterative—adjustments are made by refining the instructions rather than the code.
Acceptance Without Full Understanding : True “vibe coding” means embracing the AI’s suggestions without thorough manual review or understanding of the codebase, in contrast to traditional pair programming or code-completion tools where the developer remains tightly involved with the output.
Faster Prototyping : Vibe coding accelerates app building, making it possible for those with less coding experience to develop complex software rapidly.
Risks and Criticisms : While this method opens software development to more people and speeds up prototyping, there are concerns about maintainability, accountability, and security—especially since developers might deploy code they do not fully understand.

title: AI-Agenter-F2026
text:
Typical Vibe Coding Workflow
State what’s needed in plain English
Let the AI generate, test, and refine the code
Repeat and iterate by updating prompts or goals
Focus on output and function, not on syntax or structure

Access to Up-to-Date Information: Unlike static models, RAG allows AI to provide recent, domain-specific, or company-private data without retraining.

RAG Architecture and Process
Indexing/Preparation : External data is pre-processed and turned into numerical embeddings (vectors), often stored in a vector database for efficient retrieval.
Retrieval : On receiving a query, the system converts the query into an embedding and retrieves relevant documents or data chunks from the vector store.
Augmentation : The retrieved information is placed in the prompt using prompt engineering templates, making it available to the model during generation.
Generation : The LLM produces its output by combining its internal knowledge with the retrieved, up-to-date context, leading to more truthful and current responses

How to Train a Neural Network

Initialize Weights : Start by assigning small, random values to all weights in the network.
Forward Propagation : Feed the network a known input to produce an output or a prediction.
Calculate Loss : Compare the network’s output to the correct output to determine the error.
Backpropagation & Weight Adjustment : Calculate how much each weight contributed to the error, and adjust the weights to reduce this error.
Iterate : Repeat this process many times, allowing the network to gradually improve its accuracy by continuously refining its weights.

Self-Attention
Self-attention allows a model to weigh the importance of different words in a sentence when processing a particular word

For example: “The robot picked up the red ball because it was the right color,”self-attention helps the model understand that “it” refers to the “ball” and not the “robot.” 

For each word, the model can “look” at all other words in the input sequence and determine which ones are most relevant to understanding its meaning in that specific context
This ability to capture relationships between words, regardless of their distance from each other in the sentence, is a key advantage over sequential models

Encoder (left): The encoder receives an input and builds a representation of it (its features). This means that the model is optimized to acquire understanding from the input.
Decoder (right): The decoder uses the encoder’s representation (features) along with other inputs to generate a target sequence. This means that the model is optimized for generating outputs.

title: AI-Agenter-F2026
text:
LLM  limitations
Hallucinations : LLMs can generate plausible but incorrect or nonsensical information.[23]
Bias : They can reflect and amplify biases present in their training data.
Lack of True Understanding : At their core, LLMs are probabilistic models predicting the next token; they do not possess true consciousness or understanding in the human sense.
Computational Cost : Training and deploying large-scale LLMs requires significant computational resources.

title: AI-Agenter-F2026
text:
Temperature
Temperature is a key parameter that controls the randomness of an LLM’s output.
It’s a value, typically between 0 and 2, that you can set when you make a request to the model.
Think of it as a dial for creativity.
Low Temperature (e.g., 0.1 to 0.5): With a low temperature, the model becomes more deterministic and conservative.
High Temperature (e.g., 0.8 to 1.5): A higher temperature increases the chances of the model selecting less likely tokens.

title: AI-Agenter-F2026
text:
More temperature
Not True Creativity : While a higher temperature can lead to more novel-sounding outputs, it’s not the same as human creativity. It’s simply increasing the mathematical randomness of the word selection.[10][15] The model’s inherent creativity is more tied to its architecture and training data.[15]
Risk of Incoherence : Pushing the temperature too high can result in nonsensical or “hallucinated” outputs that don’t make sense.[7]
Finding the Balance : The right temperature setting depends entirely on the task at hand. For a reliable AI agent performing a predictable task, a low temperature is generally preferred.[10] For an agent designed to brainstorm or explore possibilities, a higher temperature might be more appropriate.[9]

FORMÅL OG LÆRINGSMÅL

AI Agenter er avanceret AI, som selvstændigt finder strategi og løsning på komplekse opgaver. LLMer (som ChatGTP) er AI som mennesker kan chatte med og få svar, mens en AI Agent selvstændigt udfører opgaver. En AI agent har adgang til systemer og værktøjer, som den bruger til at udføre opgaver automatisk.​ ​
På kurset lærer du at opsætte workflows til automatisering af opgaver, som spænder fra at få daglige nyheder om f.eks. AI agenter, til et større SOME marketings setup. Du vil lære om hvordan large language models (som ChatGPT) virker og at bruge dem til AI agenter. Du vil lære prompt engineering til instruere AI agenterne til at udføre deres opgaver. Derudover kigger vi på RAGs, hvor AI får information fra vector databaser til deres opgaver​
Vi bruger workflow værktøjet n8n til at sætte vores agenter og workflows op. Der vil være behov en smule JavaScript, hvor det meste dog kan fås fra diverse LLMer uden de store problemer. Der vil være mulighed for at bruge Python e.lign programmeringssprog i det afsluttende projekt, men det er ikke et krav.

title: AI-Agenter-F2026
text:
Chain-of-Thought ( CoT ) Reasoning
A method that guides the model to break down a complex problem into a series of “intermediate reasoning steps” that logically lead to a final answer
This approach simulates a human-like problem-solving process and is particularly effective for tasks involving arithmetic, commonsense, and symbolic reasoning
“Zero-Shot CoT” - “Let’s think this through step by step”

Can unlock sophisticated problem-solving capacity within the model

The capacity to “think out loud” provides an interpretable window into the model’s behavior, allowing developers to debug where a reasoning path may have gone wrong.

e.g. a math problem where the model shows its work
Provides a more  transparrent and trustworthy final output

title: AI-Agenter-F2026
text:
Tree-of-Thought ( ToT ) Exploration
ToT explores multiple reasoning paths in parallel, structuring the problem-solving process like a decision tree
This approach allows the model to brainstorm different potential solutions, evaluate each one, and even backtrack if a particular path proves to be unproductive

RAGs  addresses a core limitation of LLMs: their reliance on static training data, which can be outdated or lack domain-specific information
RAG mitigates this by grounding the model’s responses in external, up-to-date knowledge

Access to Up-to-Date Information: Unlike static models, RAG allows AI to provide recent, domain-specific, or company-private data without retraining.

title: AI-Agenter-F2026
text:
RAG Architecture and Process
Indexing/Preparation : External data is pre-processed and turned into numerical embeddings (vectors), often stored in a vector database for efficient retrieval.
Retrieval : On receiving a query, the system converts the query into an embedding and retrieves relevant documents or data chunks from the vector store.
Augmentation : The retrieved information is placed in the prompt using prompt engineering templates, making it available to the model during generation.
Generation : The LLM produces its output by combining its internal knowledge with the retrieved, up-to-date context, leading to more truthful and current responses

Embeddings are numerical representations of text, allowing models to compare meaning and context.
Example: “Coffee” and “Espresso” have similar embeddings; “Coffee” and “Cat” are far apart
These representations are stored in a vector database

Studieordningen
FORMÅL OG LÆRINGSMÅL
AI Agenter er avanceret AI, som selvstændigt finder strategi og løsning på komplekse opgaver. LLMer (som ChatGPT) er AI som mennesker kan chatte med og få svar, mens en AI Agent selvstændigt udfører opgaver. En AI agent har adgang til systemer og værktøjer, som den bruger til at udføre opgaver automatisk.​ ​
På kurset lærer du at opsætte workflows til automatisering af opgaver, som spænder fra at få daglige nyheder om f.eks. AI agenter, til et større SOME marketings setup. Du vil lære om hvordan large language models (som ChatGPT) virker og at bruge dem til AI agenter. Du vil lære prompt engineering til instruere AI agenterne til at udføre deres opgaver. Derudover kigger vi på RAGs, hvor AI får information fra vector databaser til deres opgaver​
​ Vi bruger workflow værktøjet n8n til at sætte vores agenter og workflows op. Der vil være behov en smule JavaScript, hvor det meste dog kan fås fra diverse LLMer uden de store problemer. Der vil være mulighed for at bruge Python e.lign programmeringssprog i det afsluttende projekt, men det er ikke et krav.

title: 1. AI agenter og automatisering
text:
Large Language model

An LLM is a type of Artificial Intelligence trained on vast amounts of text data to understand, generate, and manipulate human language.
To break it down:

Large: Refers to the scale of the training data (petabytes of text) and the complexity of the model (billions of “parameters”).
Language: It is built to process communication—not just English or Danish, but also computer code and mathematical logic. Model: It is a complex mathematical representation of patterns found in human thought and speech.

title: 1. AI agenter og automatisering
text:
LLM
An LLM is a highly advanced statistical autocomplete. It doesn’t ‘know’ facts like a person does; instead, it predicts the next most likely word (token) in a sequence based on everything it has ever read.

What is an AI Agent?


The “Wrapper” Concept

We place a software layer around the LLM.
LLM = The Brain.
Software = The Body.

title: 1. AI agenter og automatisering
text:
What is an AI Agent?


Key Capabilities:

Reasoning: Planning steps to a goal.
Memory: Remembering past context.
Tools: Interacting with APIs/Databases.

title: 1. AI agenter og automatisering
text:
Example: The Meeting Booking Agent
The Goal: “Schedule a 30-minute sync with Peter next Tuesday afternoon.”


Chatbot (Passive)

User: “Book a meeting with Peter.”
Bot: “Tells you to look up in the calendars and send invite to Peter.”
Result: User has to do the work.


AI Agent (Active)

User: “Book a meeting with Peter.”
Agent: Searches contacts for Peter, checks your calendar, emails Peter options, and creates the invite.
Result: Task Completed.

title: 1. AI agenter og automatisering
text:
How the Agent Thinks
When you give the command, the Agent enters a Thought-Action-Observation loop:

Thought: I need to find Peter’s email address.

Action: Search CRM/Contacts tool for “Peter.”
Observation: Found peter@company.com.

Thought: I need to find free slots on Tuesday afternoon.

Action: Check Google Calendar for Tuesday between 13:00 and 17:00.
Observation: User is free at 14:00 and 15:30.

Thought: I will propose these times to Peter via email.

Action: Send email to Peter via Gmail tool.
Observation: Email sent successfully.

Final Response: “I’ve reached out to Peter with two options for Tuesday afternoon.”

title: 1. AI agenter og automatisering
text:
The Agent’s “Hands” (Tools)
To book that meeting, the Agent was connected to these n8n nodes:

Google Contacts: To find the right person.
Google Calendar: To read availability and write the event.
Gmail / Outlook: To communicate with the external party.
LLM (The Brain): To decide which tool to use and what to write.

title: 1. AI agenter og automatisering
text:
The “Recipe” Analogy

The Business Process: “Making Dinner for 10 People” (The high-level goal).
The Workflow: “The Recipe for Lasagna” (The specific, repeatable steps).

A Workflow must be: {.fragment} - Explicit: No guessing. Every step is defined. - Repeatable: If you follow the recipe exactly, you get the same meal every time. - Automatable: Once the recipe is clear, a “robot chef” (n8n) can do the cooking for you.

title: 1. AI agenter og automatisering
text:
Agents need workflows

An LLM (Agent) might know how to write an email, but it doesn’t know when to send it, where to get the email address, or how to log the activity in a database.
The Workflow is the skeleton that gives the Agent a purpose and access to the real world.
We don’t just build AI Agents to have a conversation. We build Workflows to give those Agents a job to do.

title: 1. AI agenter og automatisering
text:
Deterministic vs. Agentic Workflows


Deterministic
The Traditional Way - Rules-based: “If This, Then That.” - Fixed Paths: Every step is pre-defined. - Predictable: Given the same input, you always get the same output. - Analogy: A train on tracks.

Agentic
The AI-Powered Way - Goal-based: “Find the answer to X.” - Dynamic Paths: The AI decides which tools to use in real-time. - Flexible: Can handle unexpected data or “fuzzy” logic. - Analogy: A taxi driver.

text:
The n8n “Superpower”


We build deterministic workflows that use AI Agents as “intelligent stops” along the way.

n8n

n8n is an open-source, node-based workflow automation tool that enables users to connect various apps and services to automate tasks without extensive coding (No-code/low-code).

Automates complex workflows by connecting APIs, databases, and cloud services.
Offers a visual, drag-and-drop interface to build workflows.

Self-hostable, providing data privacy and control.
Integrates with hundreds of applications out-of-the-box.
Useful for automating repetitive tasks, data synchronization, and alerts.

text:
How to Install n8n Locally
You have two main paths to run n8n on your own computer. Both are free and private.


Option A: Docker (Recommended)

Pros: Isolated environment, easy to backup, professional standard.
Cons: Requires installing Docker Desktop first.


Option B: npx / npm

Pros: Instant start if you already have Node.js.
Cons: Brittle; if you close the terminal, n8n stops. Harder to manage long-term.

title: 1. AI agenter og automatisering
text:
Running n8n (Mac & Linux)
Copy and paste this command into your terminal to run n8n in the background:
docker run -d \
  --name n8n \
  -p 5678:5678 \
  -v ~/.n8n:/home/node/.n8n \
  n8nio/n8n






Note


The -v ~/.n8n:/home/node/.n8n part ensures your workflows are saved in your user’s home folder.

title: 1. AI agenter og automatisering
text:
Running n8n (Windows PowerShell)
docker run -d `
  --name n8n `
  -p 5678:5678 `
  -v ${env:USERPROFILE}\.n8n:/home/node/.n8n `
  n8nio/n8n

title: 1. AI agenter og automatisering
text:
Why these specific flags?

-d (Detached): Runs the container in the background. You can close your terminal and n8n will keep running.
--name n8n: Gives the container a friendly name so you don’t have to remember a random ID.
-p 5678:5678: Maps the internal n8n port to your computer’s port.
-v (Volume): The most important part. This links a folder on your computer to n8n. Without this, your work vanishes when the container stops.

title: 1. AI agenter og automatisering
text:

Access: http://localhost:5678
Stop: docker stop n8n
Start: docker start n8n
Update:

docker pull n8nio/n8n
docker stop n8n && docker rm n8n
Run the “docker run” command again.

A good tool should be something that complements the power of an LLM .

Arguments with typings.

Temperature

Temperature is a key parameter that controls the randomness of an LLM’s output.
It’s a value, typically between 0 and 2, that you can set when you make a request to the model.
Think of it as a dial for creativity.
Low Temperature (e.g., 0.1 to 0.5): With a low temperature, the model becomes more deterministic and conservative.
High Temperature (e.g., 0.8 to 1.5): A higher temperature increases the chances of the model selecting less likely tokens.

title: 5. Prompt engineering - vibe coding
text:
More temperature

Not True Creativity : While a higher temperature can lead to more novel-sounding outputs, it’s not the same as human creativity. It’s simply increasing the mathematical randomness of the word selection.[10][15] The model’s inherent creativity is more tied to its architecture and training data.[15]
Risk of Incoherence : Pushing the temperature too high can result in nonsensical or “hallucinated” outputs that don’t make sense.[7]
Finding the Balance : The right temperature setting depends entirely on the task at hand. For a reliable AI agent performing a predictable task, a low temperature is generally preferred.[10] For an agent designed to brainstorm or explore possibilities, a higher temperature might be more appropriate.[9]

title: 5. Prompt engineering - vibe coding
text:
Top-K Sampling


Definition: Filters the probability distribution to keep only the top k most likely tokens.
Process:

Sort all possible next words by their probability.
Keep only the top k options (e.g., if k=40, only the 40 most likely words are considered).
Redistribute the probability mass among these k tokens.
Randomly sample the next word from this restricted set.

Impact:

Pros: Very simple and prevents the model from picking completely nonsensical “long-tail” words.
Cons: It is not adaptive. If the model is very confident (one word is 99%), it still looks at the other 39. If the model is uncertain, it might cut off valid, high-quality choices.

title: 5. Prompt engineering - vibe coding
text:
Top-P (Nucleus) Sampling


Definition: A dynamic approach that selects the smallest set of tokens whose cumulative probability exceeds a threshold p.
Process:

Sort all possible next words by probability.
Add words to a “nucleus” one by one until their combined probability reaches p (e.g., p=0.9 or 90%).
The number of words in the set grows or shrinks based on the model’s confidence.
Sample the next word only from this “nucleus.”

Impact:

Pros: Adaptive. When the model is confident, the set is small (maybe 1 word); when it’s confused, the set is large.
Cons: Harder to predict exactly how many options the model will have at any given step.

Often considered superior to Top-K for maintaining a natural and creative “flow” in conversation.

title: 7. Vector RAG
text:
RAG Architecture and Process

Indexing/Preparation: External data is pre-processed and turned into numerical embeddings (vectors), often stored in a vector database for efficient retrieval.
Retrieval: On receiving a query, the system converts the query into an embedding and retrieves relevant documents or data chunks from the vector store.
Augmentation: The retrieved information is placed in the prompt using prompt engineering templates, making it available to the model during generation.
Generation: The LLM produces its output by combining its internal knowledge with the retrieved, up-to-date context, leading to more truthful and current responses.

title: 7. Vector RAG
text:
Embeddings (Indexing/Preparation)

Embeddings are numerical representations of text, allowing models to compare meaning and context.
Example: “Coffee” and “Espresso” have similar embeddings; “Coffee” and “Cat” are far apart.
These representations are stored in a vector database.

title: 7. Vector RAG
section: Why Do We Need Embeddings in RAG?
text:
Why Do We Need Embeddings in RAG?

Problem: Pure keyword search can miss context and semantic meaning.
Embeddings power semantic search: retrieve relevant content even if different words are used.
Embeddings make RAG powerful and accurate.

title: 7. Vector RAG
text:
Exercise: Manual Embeddings
Can you embed words by hand?

Draw a 2D coordinate system with two axes — you decide what they mean!

e.g. x = size (small → large), y = domestic → wild

Place these words on your map:

🐱 cat, 🐶 dog, 🐯 tiger, 🐻 bear, 🐹 hamster, 🦁 lion, 🐕 wolf, 🐇 rabbit

Compare with your neighbour — do you agree?
Which of the other animals ended up closest to “cat” on your map?

What does that tell us about their relationship?



This is exactly what real embeddings do — but in hundreds or thousands dimensions instead of 2!

title: 7. Vector RAG
text:
Debrief: What did we learn?

Axes matter: the dimensions we choose shape the “meaning”
Real embeddings learn their axes from billions of words — we just made them up
Key insight: similarity = distance. Close = related. Far = different.
A vector DB just asks: “what’s closest to this query vector?”
Think of a vector DB as a filter on your data

title: 7. Vector RAG
text:
Embedding Models

We placed words manually — in reality, specialised LLMs do this automatically
Called embedding models — trained specifically to convert text into vectors
Examples: text-embedding-ada-002 (OpenAI), nomic-embed-text, mxbai-embed
Different from chat models — they don’t generate text, they output numbers
You need to use the same model for indexing and querying

title: 7. Vector RAG
text:
Semantic Search Basics
Keyword search: matches your exact words - Search “car repair” → finds “car repair”. Search “fixing automobiles” → finds nothing.
Semantic search: understands what you mean - Search “fixing automobiles” → still finds the car repair docs, because the meaning is the same.

Your query is turned into a vector
Stored documents are also vectors
Finds the ones pointing in the same “direction” — closest in meaning

title: 7. Vector RAG
text:
The Embedding Workflow in n8n

Fetch data (text files, docs, etc.)
Use n8n’s embedding node to convert text chunks into vectors.
Optionally, enrich with metadata (title, source, section).
Store vectors in a vector database like NEO4J (several others out there).

title: 7. Vector RAG
text:
Why NEO4J for RAG?

Graph + Vector in one: combine semantic search with graph traversal
Uses its own Cypher query language
Three query modes in one DB:

Cypher — graph queries
Vector index — semantic similarity search
Full-text index — keyword search (Lucene)

title: 7. Vector RAG
text:
NEO4J Vector: Core Concepts
Node — your data unit (a chunk of text)
(:Chunk {
  id: "week1-chunk-0",
  text: "AI agents perceive and act...",
  embedding: [0.12, -0.34, ...],  // 768 floats
  source: "week1-slides.md",
  week: 1
})

title: 7. Vector RAG
text:
NEO4J Vector: Core Concepts II
Vector Index — tells NEO4J which property to search
CREATE VECTOR INDEX course_chunks
FOR (n:Chunk) ON n.embedding
OPTIONS { indexConfig: {
  `vector.dimensions`: 768,
  `vector.similarity_function`: 'cosine'
}}

Speed: uses HNSW algorithm to find similar vectors fast — without it Neo4j compares every node one by one

Hierarchical Navigable Small World (HNSW) — a graph-based algorithm for fast nearest-neighbor search.

Scope: defines which nodes are searchable — queryNodes(‘course_chunks’, …) only searches nodes registered in that index

title: 7. Vector RAG
text:
NEO4J Vector: Query
Retrieval — embed your question, find closest chunks
CALL db.index.vector.queryNodes(
  'course_chunks',   -- index name
  3,                 -- top K results
  $embedding         -- your query vector
)
YIELD node, score
RETURN node.text, node.source, node.week, score

Returns chunks ranked by cosine similarity
Score close to 1.0 = very similar
Score close to 0.0 = unrelated

title: 7. Vector RAG
text:
The Full Pipeline
Your files (MD + transcripts)
  ↓
n8n: Read file → Chunk text
  ↓
n8n: Ollama (nomic-embed-text) → 768-dim vector
  ↓
n8n: HTTP POST → NEO4J insert Chunk node
  ↓
Vector Index (automatic)
  ↓
AI Agent: question → embed → queryNodes → answer

title: 13. MCP servers
text:
MCP - Model Context Protocol - recap
MCP (Model Context Protocol) is an open standard that lets AI applications discover and use external data sources, tools, and workflows through a common interface.

title: 13. MCP servers
text: MCP examples

title: 13. MCP servers
text:
Why does MCP matter?

Developers: MCP reduces development time and complexity when building, or integrating with, an AI application or agent.
AI applications or agents: MCP provides access to an ecosystem of data sources, tools and apps which will enhance capabilities and improve the end-user experience.
End-users: MCP results in more capable AI applications or agents which can access your data and take actions on your behalf when necessary.

title: 13. MCP servers
text:
MCP vs. API



Discovery – ask the MCP for its tools
Unlike traditional APIs, where every integration is custom, MCP standardizes the interface.
An AI agent can interact with any MCP-compatible service without needing prior knowledge of its specifics.
API creates breaking changes. MCP can be used immediately after a change.

title: 13. MCP servers
text:
Two Core Problems MCP Solves

LLMs need two things from external systems:

Context — Structured data (documents, database records, knowledge bases).
Tools — Actions they can perform (search the web, send an email, run code).

Feedback on project

Groups of three
One person present project for the others

title: 13. MCP servers
text:
Give feedback

Den er beskrivende frem for vurderende. Ved at beskrive sine egne reaktioner, giver man det andet menneske frihed til selv at bruge informationen på den måde, han ønsker. Ved at undgå vurderende udtryk, reduceres den andens behov for at forsvare sig. ”Du mødte en halv time for sent i dag og 20 minutter for sent mandag” er et eksempel på en beskrivende feedback. ”Du er sløv” er modsat et eksempel på en vurderende feedback.
Den er specifik og ikke generel.”Jeg sætter pris på, at du altid laver et kort og klart referat af mødet, men jeg synes det ville være rart, hvis du ville sende mødeindkaldelsen ud senest 3 dage før mødet. Jeg vil også gerne, at du sørger for, at vi holder os til talelisten, hvor jeg i dag oplever at især Knud og Hans får lov at bryde ind i, når det passer dem” er et eksempel på en specifik feedback, medens ”Jeg synes, din mødeledelse er for slap” er et eksempel på en generel feedback, som man næppe kan gøre andet ved end forsvare sig imod.

title: 13. MCP servers
text:
Give feedback II

Den udtrykkes i jeg-form. Det er langt lettere at modtage feed back, hvor afsenderen tager udgangspunkt i egne holdninger og følelser. ”Jeg bliver irriteret og vred, når du ikke overholder vores aftaler”, er en feed back som tager udgangspunkt i afsenderens følelser. Mens ”det er for dårligt, at du ikke overholder vores aftaler” er en feed back, der formuleres som en generel sandhed, og som let vækker større modstand.
Den er rettet mod adfærd, som modtageren kan gøre noget ved (hvis han/hun ønsker det) Man øger kun frustrationen hos en person, når man oplyser ham om mangler, som han ingen kontrol har over. At kritisere fx tøj-smag vil næppe medføre den ønskede adfærdsændring hos modtageren.

title: 13. MCP servers
text:
Give feedback III

Den er ønsket, og ikke påtvunget. Feedback er mest nyttig, når modtageren selv har udtrykt ønske om at modtage den. Man kan fx spørge: ”Er du interesseret i at få feed back på din håndtering af salgsmødet?” frem for blot at gå i gang med at analysere salgsmødet for kollegaen.
Kommer ofte hurtigt efter den pågældende adfærd, som den beskriver, dog afhængig af, om personen er parat til at høre den, og om evt. andre tilstedeværende bør høre med. Umiddelbar feed back har den fordel, at parterne lettere kan huske hvad der foregik, og man undgår at gå og ”ruge” over sagen.

title: 13. MCP servers
text:
Give feedback IV

Den giver plads til dialog. Modtagerens motivation for at udvikle sig øges, hvis der er plads til uddybning og afklaring, og til at diskutere løsningsmuligheder. Lad fx være med at give feed back via e-mailen.
Den er fremadrettet.God feed back er fremadrettet og vil ofte indeholde forslag til, hvordan adfærden kan ændres. ”Jeg synes, det ville være dejligt, hvis du begyndte at sige godmorgen til os andre, når du møder om morgenen” er en konstruktiv og fremadrettet feed back.

title: 13. MCP servers
text:
Modtage feedback

Lyt til feed back’en, som den bliver fremstillet (undgå at argumentere imod feed back’en, fokuser på det, der faktisk bliver sagt).
Lyt aktivt: Få giveren til at uddybe sine meninger og observationer, hold øjenkontakt.
Hold dig til sagen (undgå at skifte emne eller gå til modangreb).
Gør det klart, at du har forstået budskabet
Undersøg efterfølgende hos andre, om de har gjort tilsvarende observationer.
